title: Lecture #35: Java Queue Interface Deep Dive

questions.question: On an EMPTY queue, which pair of `Queue` methods returns `null` instead of throwing an exception?
options: `add()` and `remove()`
`element()` and `remove()`
`poll()` and `peek()`
`offer()` and `element()`
questions.explanation: Queue offers each operation in two styles: `add`/`remove`/`element` throw an exception on failure, while `offer`/`poll`/`peek` return a special value (false or null) — the lecture's "safer alternatives". So `poll()` (remove head) and `peek()` (look at head) return null on an empty queue, whereas `remove()` and `element()` throw `NoSuchElementException`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A Queue is FIFO: `poll()` removes and returns the head, 1. `peek()` only looks at the new head, 2, without removing it, so two elements remain. The "3 2 2" option treats the queue like a LIFO stack, and "1 2 3" forgets that `poll()` actually removed an element.

questions.question: A teammate's code calls `queue.offer(null)` on a `Queue` created as `new ArrayDeque<>()` and gets a `NullPointerException`. The same call worked when the queue was a `LinkedList`. Why?
options: `offer` never accepts null on any Queue; the LinkedList version must have used `add`
ArrayDeque does not allow null elements, while LinkedList does
ArrayDeque is full and throws NullPointerException to signal that capacity is exhausted
ArrayDeque is a legacy class that only accepts objects of type Integer
questions.explanation: The lecture notes it directly: ArrayDeque → null not allowed, LinkedList → null allowed. Disallowing null makes sense because `poll()`/`peek()` use null to mean "the queue is empty". ArrayDeque grows automatically, so capacity is not the issue, and it is a modern class, not a legacy one.

questions.question: A min-heap is stored in an array as `[10, 30, 20, 40, 50]` (indexes 0–4). Using the lecture's rules (left = 2i+1, right = 2i+2), which elements are the children of 30?
options: 20 and 40
10 and 20
There are none, because 30 is a leaf
40 and 50
questions.explanation: 30 is at index 1, so its children are at 2·1+1 = 3 and 2·1+2 = 4, which hold 40 and 50. A binary heap is a complete binary tree, which is why it can be packed into an array with no gaps and navigated with this index arithmetic. 20 is 30's sibling (index 2), not its child.

questions.question: This PriorityQueue is built with the comparator from the lecture's Demo2. What does it print?
questions.explanation: The comparator `(a, b) -> b - a` reverses natural order, turning the default min-heap into a max-heap, so the largest element is always at the head. Two polls remove 50 and 40, and `peek()` shows the next largest, 30, without removing it. "10 20 30" is what the default (min-heap) PriorityQueue would give.

questions.question: An `ArrayDeque` is used both as a stack and from the other end. What does this print? (`toString` lists elements from first to last.)
questions.explanation: For a Deque used as a stack, `push` inserts at the front, so after three pushes the deque is [3, 2, 1]; `offerLast(4)` appends at the back: [3, 2, 1, 4]. `pop` removes from the front and returns 3, leaving [2, 1, 4], and `peekLast()` reads 4 without removing it. The first option wrongly assumes push/pop work at the back.

questions.question: In a hospital emergency system, patients arrive over time and each has a severity score; the doctor must always treat the most severe waiting patient next, not whoever arrived first. Which collection fits?
options: A `PriorityQueue<Patient>` ordered by severity (highest first)
An `ArrayDeque<Patient>` used as a FIFO queue
An `ArrayDeque<Patient>` used as a LIFO stack
A `LinkedList<Patient>` scanned from the front each time
questions.explanation: A PriorityQueue is not FIFO: `poll()` always removes the highest-priority element according to its ordering, which with a severity comparator is the most severe patient. ArrayDeque gives arrival order (FIFO) or reverse arrival order (LIFO), neither of which reflects severity. Scanning a LinkedList each time works but costs O(n) per pick instead of O(log n).

questions.question: A default (min-heap) PriorityQueue is printed before and after one `poll()`. `toString` shows the internal array order. What is printed?
questions.explanation: Each insert is placed at the end and up-heapified only while it is smaller than its parent; none of these inserts beats its parent, so the array stays [10, 30, 20, 40, 50] — a valid heap, but not sorted. `poll()` removes the root, moves the last element (50) to the root and down-heapifies it: it swaps with the smaller child 20, giving [20, 30, 50, 40]. Only repeated `poll()` calls return elements in sorted order; printing the queue does not.

questions.question: Both `ArrayDeque` and `LinkedList` implement `Deque` and add/remove at either end in O(1). Why does the lecture still prefer ArrayDeque for queues and stacks?
options: Because LinkedList's `addFirst` is O(n), since it must shift all elements
Because ArrayDeque stores elements in a contiguous (circular) array, which is cache-friendly and avoids allocating a node object per element
Because ArrayDeque is synchronized and therefore safe for multiple threads
Because ArrayDeque keeps elements sorted, which makes `peek()` faster
questions.explanation: Both have O(1) end operations, so the difference is constant factors: ArrayDeque uses one contiguous circular array with front/rear indexes (resizing when full), which the CPU cache handles well, while LinkedList allocates a separate node with prev/next pointers for each element. LinkedList's ends are O(1) too — no shifting happens. ArrayDeque is neither synchronized nor sorted.

questions.question: A stream of 1,000,000 prices arrives one by one, and after each arrival the app needs the current minimum. A teammate appends to an ArrayList and sorts it after every insert. What does switching to a `PriorityQueue` give you?
options: Nothing — a PriorityQueue also re-sorts all elements on every `offer`, so the cost is the same
O(1) `offer` and O(1) `poll`, because the heap is stored in an array
`offer` in O(log n) via up-heapify and `peek` of the minimum in O(1), instead of an O(n log n) sort per insert
O(log n) `peek`, because the minimum must be searched for in the tree
questions.explanation: A binary heap only restores the parent-child order along one root-to-leaf path: inserting walks up (up-heapify) and removing walks down (down-heapify), both O(log n). The minimum always sits at the root, so `peek()` is O(1). Re-sorting the whole list after each insert is O(n log n) per element; the heap never fully sorts its array.
